title: Chapter 10. Of Power, Worth, Dignity, Honour and Worthiness
paragraphs: The POWER of a man, taken in its widest sense, is his present means to obtain some future apparent good. It is either original or instrumental.

Natural power is the eminence of the faculties of body or mind: extraordinary strength, good looks, prudence, the arts, eloquence, generosity, nobility. Instrumental powers are those that, having been acquired by natural powers or by fortune, then serve as means and instruments for acquiring more — riches, reputation, friends, and the secret working of God which men call Good Luck. The nature of power, on this point, is like fame: it grows as it goes; or like the motion of heavy bodies, which the further they travel, the more they accelerate.

The greatest of human powers is the one compounded of the powers of many men, united by consent in one person, natural or civil, who has the use of all their powers at his will — such as the power of a commonwealth — or united by depending on the wills of each individual member, such as the power of a faction, or of several factions allied. So to have servants is power; to have friends is power; both are united strengths.
Riches joined with generosity are power, because they win friends and servants. Without generosity they are not power: in that case they do not defend, but expose a man to envy, like prey.
The reputation of power is power, because it draws to it the loyalty of those who need protection.
So too is the reputation of love for one's country — what is called popularity — for the same reason.
Likewise, any quality whatever that makes a man loved or feared by many, or the reputation of such a quality, is power, because it is a means to gain the help and service of many.
Success is power, because it builds a reputation of wisdom or of good fortune, which makes men either fear a man or rely on him.
Affability in men already in power is an increase of power, because it earns affection.
A reputation for prudence in the conduct of peace or war is power, because the government of ourselves is entrusted more willingly to prudent men than to others.
Nobility is power not everywhere, but only in those commonwealths where it carries privileges; for those privileges are what its power consists in.
Eloquence is power, because it has the appearance of prudence.
Good looks are power, because being a promise of good, they recommend a man to the favour of women and of strangers.

The sciences are little power, because they are not eminent and so are not noticed in any man; in fact they exist hardly at all except in a few people, and even in them only on a few subjects. Science is of such a nature that no one can recognize it for what it is unless he has himself attained it in good measure.

Arts of public use — fortification, the making of engines and other instruments of war — are power, because they contribute to defence and victory. And though the true mother of these arts is science (specifically mathematics), since they are brought into the light by the hand of the craftsman, they are credited to him as his offspring: the midwife passes, with the common people, for the mother.

The value, or WORTH, of a man is, as with all other things, his price — that is, what would be given for the use of his power; and so it is not absolute, but depends on the need and the judgement of another. An able commander of soldiers carries a high price in time of war, present or imminent, but not so in peace. A learned and incorruptible judge is worth much in time of peace, but not so much in war. And as in other things, so in men, it is not the seller but the buyer who sets the price. For let a man (as most men do) rate himself at the highest value he can — his real value is no more than what others estimate it to be.

The way we show the value we set on each other is what is commonly called honouring and dishonouring. To value a man at a high rate is to honour him; at a low rate, to dishonour him. But 'high' and 'low' here are to be understood by comparison with the rate each man sets on himself.

The public worth of a man, which is the value set on him by the commonwealth, is what men commonly call DIGNITY. This value placed on a man by the commonwealth is signalled by offices of command, of judgement, or of public employment, or by names and titles introduced to mark out such value.
To beg another for help of any kind is to honour him, because it is a sign of one's opinion that he has the power to help; and the more difficult the help required, the greater the honour.
To obey is to honour, because no one obeys those they think have no power to help or hurt them. Consequently, to disobey is to dishonour.

To give large gifts to a man is to honour him, because it is the buying of protection and the acknowledgement of power. To give small gifts is to dishonour him, because it is mere alms and signals an opinion that he needs only small helps. To be diligent in promoting another's good, and likewise to flatter him, is to honour him, as a sign that we are seeking his protection or his aid. To neglect him is to dishonour him.
To yield place or precedence to another in any matter is to honour him, as it is a confession of his greater power. To arrogate place to oneself is to dishonour him.

To show any sign of love or fear of another is to honour him; for both to love and to fear are to value. To despise him, or to love or fear him less than he expects, is to dishonour him; for that is to undervalue him.
To praise, to magnify, or to call happy is to honour, because nothing but goodness, power, and felicity is valued. To revile, to mock, or to pity is to dishonour.

To speak to another with consideration, to appear before him with decency and humility, is to honour him, as signs of fear to offend. To speak to him rashly, or to do anything before him obscenely, slovenly, or impudently, is to dishonour him.
To believe, to trust, to rely on another is to honour him; it is a sign of one's opinion of his virtue and power. To distrust, or not believe, is to dishonour.

To listen to a man's counsel, or to his discourse of any kind, is to honour him, as a sign that we think him wise, or eloquent, or witty. To fall asleep, to walk out, or to talk during it is to dishonour.

To do for another the things he takes as signs of honour, or that law or custom makes such signs, is to honour him; because by approving the honour that others do him, one acknowledges the power that they acknowledge. To refuse to do these things is to dishonour.

To agree with someone in opinion is to honour him, as a sign of approving his judgement and his wisdom. To dissent is to dishonour, and is the reproach of error — and, if the dissent is on many points, of folly.
To imitate is to honour, for it is to approve emphatically. To imitate one's enemy is to dishonour him.
To honour those whom another honours is to honour him, as a sign of approving his judgement. To honour his enemies is to dishonour him.

To employ a man in counsel, or in actions of difficulty, is to honour him, as a sign of one's opinion of his wisdom or of some other power he has. To deny such employment to those who seek it is to dishonour them.

All these ways of honouring are natural, and exist both within and outside of commonwealths. But in commonwealths, where the person or persons holding supreme authority can make whatever they please count as a sign of honour, there are also other honours.
A sovereign honours a subject with whatever title, office, employment, or action he himself wishes to have taken as a sign of his will to honour him.

The king of Persia honoured Mordecai when he ordered that he be led through the streets in the king's own garment, on one of the king's horses, with a crown on his head, and with a prince walking before him proclaiming, 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king will honour.' And yet another king of Persia (or the same king at another time) gave one of his subjects, who had asked for permission to wear one of the royal robes as reward for some great service, leave to do so — but with the condition that he wear it as the king's fool. That was dishonour. So much for civil honours, such as magistracies, offices, titles, and in some places painted coats and escutcheons; and men honour those who have them as bearing so many marks of favour in the commonwealth — and that favour is power.
Honourable is whatever possession, action, or quality is an argument and a sign of power.
And so to be honoured, loved, or feared by many is honourable, as arguments of power. To be honoured by few, or by none, is dishonourable.

Lasting good fortune is honourable, as a sign of God's favour. Bad fortune and losses are dishonourable. Riches are honourable, for they are power. Poverty is dishonourable. Magnanimity, generosity, hope, courage, confidence are honourable, for they proceed from the awareness of power. Pusillanimity, miserliness, fear, diffidence are dishonourable.

Timely resolution — the prompt determination of what a man is to do — is honourable, as it shows a disregard for small difficulties and dangers. And irresolution is dishonourable, as a sign of overvaluing small impediments and small advantages. For when a man has weighed things as long as the time allows, and still does not resolve, the difference in weight on either side must be small; so by failing to resolve, he overvalues small things — which is pusillanimity.

All actions and speeches that proceed, or seem to proceed, from much experience, science, discretion, or wit, are honourable, for all of these are powers. Actions or words proceeding from error, ignorance, or folly are dishonourable.

Gravity, so far as it seems to come from a mind occupied with something important, is honourable, because that occupation is itself a sign of power. But if it seems to be put on for the sake of appearing grave, then it is dishonourable. The gravity of the first is like the steadiness of a ship laden with merchandise; that of the second is like the steadiness of a ship ballasted with sand and other rubbish.

To be conspicuous — that is, to be known for wealth, office, great actions, or any eminent good — is honourable, as a sign of the power that makes a man conspicuous. On the contrary, obscurity is dishonourable.

To be descended from conspicuous parents is honourable, because such a person can the more easily lay hold of the aids and friends his ancestors had. On the contrary, to be descended from obscure parentage is dishonourable.

Actions that proceed from equity, joined with personal loss, are honourable, as signs of magnanimity — for magnanimity is a sign of power. On the contrary, craft, shifting, and the neglect of equity are dishonourable.

Nor does it change the question of honour whether an action — provided it is great and difficult, and so a sign of much power — is just or unjust. Honour consists only in the opinion of power. So the ancient heathens did not think they were dishonouring their gods, but rather greatly honouring them, when they introduced them in their poems as committing rapes, thefts, and other great but unjust or unclean acts. Nothing is so much celebrated in Jupiter as his adulteries; nor in Mercury as his frauds and thefts. The greatest of Mercury's praises in a hymn of Homer is that, being born in the morning, he had invented music by noon, and before nightfall had stolen the cattle of Apollo from his herdsmen.

Likewise among men, until great commonwealths were instituted, it was thought no dishonour to be a pirate or a highwayman, but rather a lawful trade — not only among the Greeks but among all other nations, as is plain from the histories of ancient times. And in our own day, in this part of the world, private duels are, and always will be, honourable (though unlawful) until such time as honour is appointed for those who refuse them, and infamy for those who issue the challenge. For duels, too, are often the effects of courage, and the ground of courage is always strength or skill, which are forms of power; though in most cases they are the effects of rash speaking, and of the fear of dishonour in one or both of the combatants, who, having committed themselves rashly, are driven into the lists to avoid disgrace.

Escutcheons and hereditary coats of arms, where they carry some eminent privilege, are honourable; otherwise not. Their power consists either in such privileges, or in the riches, or in some other quality that would equally be honoured in other men. This kind of honour, commonly called gentry, was derived from the ancient Germans. There never was any such thing where German customs were unknown, and it is nowhere in use today except where the Germans once dwelt. The ancient Greek commanders, when they went to war, had their shields painted with whatever devices they pleased — so much so that an unpainted shield was a sign of poverty and of a common soldier — but they did not pass these devices on by inheritance. The Romans did pass on family marks, but these were the images of their ancestors, not their devices. Among the peoples of Asia, Africa, and America, no such thing exists or ever existed. Only the Germans had this custom; from them it passed to England, France, Spain, and Italy when, in great numbers, they either aided the Romans or made their own conquests in these western parts of the world.

For Germany, being in its beginnings (like all other countries) divided among countless little lords, or masters of families, who continually warred with one another, those masters or lords, mainly so that they might be known by their followers when in full armour, and partly for ornament, painted on their armour, escutcheon, or coat the figure of some beast or other object, and put some eminent and visible mark on the crest of their helmets. This ornament, on both arms and crest, passed by inheritance to their children — to the eldest unchanged, and to the rest with some mark of difference, such as the old master (in Dutch, the Herealt — the herald) thought fit. But when many such families joined together and formed a greater monarchy, this duty of the herald — distinguishing escutcheons — became a separate office. The issue of these lords is the great and ancient gentry, which for the most part bear living creatures noted for courage and rapine, or castles, battlements, belts, weapons, bars, palisades, and other marks of war; nothing being then in honour but military virtue. Later, not only kings but popular commonwealths granted various kinds of escutcheons to those who went forth to war, or returned from it, as encouragement or reward for service. All this an observing reader may find in those ancient Greek and Latin histories that treat of the German nation and its customs in their times.

Titles of honour — such as duke, count, marquis, and baron — are honourable, as they signify the value set on those bearing them by the sovereign power of the commonwealth. These titles were anciently titles of office and command, some derived from the Romans, some from the Germans and French. Dukes (in Latin duces) were generals in war; counts (comites) were those who accompanied the general out of friendship, and were left to govern and defend conquered and pacified territories; marquises (marchiones) were counts who governed the marches, or boundaries, of the Empire. These titles of duke, count, and marquis came into the Empire about the time of Constantine the Great, from the customs of the German military. But 'baron' seems to have been a Gaulish title, signifying a great man — such as the kings' or princes' men whom they employed in war about their own persons; it seems to come from Vir, becoming Ber and Bar (which in the Gaulish tongue meant what Vir meant in Latin), and so to Bero and Baro. So such men were called Berones, and later Barones, and (in Spanish) Varones. He who wants to know more about the origin of titles of honour will find it, as I have found this, in Mr Selden's excellent treatise on the subject. In the course of time these offices of honour, on account of troubles and for reasons of good and peaceful government, were turned into mere titles, serving mostly to mark the precedence, place, and order of subjects in the commonwealth; men were made dukes, counts, marquises, and barons of places where they had neither possession nor command, and other titles also were devised for the same purpose.

WORTHINESS is something different from the worth, or value, of a man, and also from his merit, or desert; it consists in a particular power or ability for the thing of which he is said to be worthy. This particular ability is usually called FITNESS, or aptitude.

For the man worthiest to be a commander, or a judge, or to have any other charge, is the one best fitted with the qualities required for discharging it well; the man worthiest of riches is the one with the qualities most needed for using them well. Any of these qualities being absent, a man may nevertheless still be a worthy man, valuable for something else. Again, a man may be worthy of riches, of office, of employment, and yet be unable to plead any right to have them ahead of another — and so cannot be said to merit or deserve them. For merit presupposes a right, and that the thing deserved is due by promise; about which I shall say more later, when I come to speak of contracts.

title: Chapter 11. Of the Difference of Manners
paragraphs: By MANNERS I do not mean here decency of behaviour — how one man ought to greet another, or how a man should rinse his mouth or pick his teeth in company, and other such points of the small moralities — but those qualities of mankind that bear on their living together in peace and unity. To this end, we should first consider that the felicity of this life does not consist in the repose of a satisfied mind. There is no such finis ultimus (utmost aim), nor summum bonum (greatest good), as the old moral philosophers' books speak of. A man whose desires have come to an end can live no more than one whose senses and imagination have come to a stop. Felicity is a continual progress of desire from one object to another, the attaining of the first being only the path to the next. The reason for this is that the object of a man's desire is not to enjoy something once, for a single instant of time, but to secure forever the way of his future desire. And so the voluntary actions and inclinations of all men aim not only at obtaining a contented life but at securing it; and they differ only in the way they go about this — a way that arises partly from the diversity of passions in different men, and partly from the difference in the knowledge or opinion each man has of the causes that produce the effect he wants.

So in the first place, I put down as a general inclination of all mankind a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ends only in death. The cause of this is not always that a man hopes for a more intense delight than he has already attained, or that he cannot be content with a moderate power, but that he cannot secure the present power and means of living well without acquiring more. And from this it follows that kings, whose power is greatest, turn their efforts to securing it — at home through laws, abroad through wars; and when that is done, a new desire succeeds: in some, the desire of fame from new conquest; in others, of ease and sensual pleasure; in others, of admiration, or of being flattered for excellence in some art or other mental ability.

Competition for riches, honour, command, or other forms of power inclines men to strife, enmity, and war. For one competitor's way of attaining his desire is to kill, subdue, supplant, or repel the other. In particular, competition for praise inclines men to a reverence for antiquity: men contend with the living, not with the dead; and they ascribe more than their due to the dead in order to dim the glory of the living.
The desire of ease and of sensual delight inclines men to obey a common power, because such desires lead a man to give up the protection that might be hoped for from his own industry and labour.

Fear of death and wounds inclines men the same way, and for the same reason. On the other hand, needy men, and hardy ones not content with their present condition, as also all men ambitious of military command, are inclined to keep the causes of war going, and to stir up trouble and sedition: for there is no military honour except by war, nor any such hope of mending a bad hand as by causing a new shuffle.

The desire of knowledge and of the arts of peace inclines men to obey a common power. Such a desire carries with it a desire for leisure, and therefore for protection by some power other than their own.

The desire for praise disposes a man to laudable actions — those that please the people whose judgement he values; for in those whom we despise, we despise their praises too. The desire for fame after death does the same. And though after death there is no sensing of the praise given us on earth — those joys being either swallowed up in the unspeakable joys of heaven or extinguished in the extreme torments of hell — yet such fame is not vain. Men get a present delight from foreseeing it, and from foreseeing the benefit that may reach their posterity through it; and though they cannot see those benefits now, they imagine them — and whatever is pleasure in the sense is pleasure in the imagination too.

To have received from one whom we regard as our equal greater benefits than there is any hope of returning disposes a man to counterfeit love, but in reality to secret hatred. It puts a man in the position of a desperate debtor who, avoiding the sight of his creditor, silently wishes him to a place where he would never have to see him again. For benefits oblige, and obligation is bondage — and bondage to one's equal is hateful. But to have received benefits from one whom we acknowledge as our superior inclines us to love, because the obligation is no new lowering of ourselves; and the cheerful acceptance of it — which men call gratitude — is itself such an honour done to the giver as is generally taken for repayment. Likewise, to receive benefits even from an equal or an inferior, so long as there is hope of returning the favour, disposes us to love. In the receiver's mind the obligation is one of mutual aid and service, and from this proceeds an emulation about who shall outdo the other in benefiting — the most noble and profitable contest possible, in which the victor is pleased with his victory and the other is satisfied by acknowledging it.
To have done more harm to a man than he can, or is willing to, make up for inclines the doer to hate the sufferer. For he must expect either revenge or forgiveness, both of which are hateful to him.
Fear of oppression disposes a man to strike first, or to seek help by joining with others; for there is no other way by which a man can secure his life and liberty.

Men who distrust their own cunning are, in tumult and sedition, better disposed for victory than those who suppose themselves wise or crafty. For the cunning love to confer; the others, fearing to be outmanoeuvred, prefer to strike first. And in sedition, where men are always on the verge of battle, holding together and using every advantage of force is a better strategy than any that can come from subtlety of wit.

Vainglorious men — those who, without being aware in themselves of any great ability, delight in supposing themselves gallant — are inclined only to display, never to attempt anything. For when danger or difficulty appears, they look for nothing but to have their incapacity exposed.

Vainglorious men of another sort — those who estimate their own ability by the flattery of others, or by the fortune of some previous action, without any sure ground of hope from a true knowledge of themselves — are inclined to commit themselves rashly, and at the approach of danger or difficulty to retreat if they can. Not seeing the way to safety, they would rather risk their honour, which can be patched up with an excuse, than their lives, for which no patch is enough.

Men who have a strong opinion of their own wisdom in matters of government are disposed to ambition. Without public employment in counsel or in magistracy, the honour of their wisdom is lost. So eloquent speakers are inclined to ambition, because eloquence has the look of wisdom both to themselves and to others.

Pusillanimity disposes men to irresolution, and so to losing the occasions and the best opportunities for action. For once men have been in deliberation right up to the point of action, if at that point it is not clear what is best to do, that is a sign that the weight of motives on each side is not far apart; and so to fail to resolve then is to lose the occasion through the weighing of trifles — which is pusillanimity.

Frugality, though a virtue in poor men, makes a man ill-suited to the kind of action that needs the strength of many men at once. It weakens their endeavour, which must be nourished and kept in vigour by reward.

Trust in others, born of ignorance of the marks of wisdom and kindness — eloquence joined with flattery — disposes men to put their confidence in those who have these things; for eloquence has the look of wisdom, flattery the look of kindness. Add a military reputation, and men are disposed to attach themselves and submit to those who have all three: the first two having reassured them against danger from him, the third reassuring them against danger from others.

Lack of science — that is, ignorance of causes — disposes, or rather forces, a man to rely on the advice and authority of others. For everyone whose interest the truth concerns, if he does not rely on his own knowledge, must rely on the opinion of someone he thinks wiser than himself and whom he sees no reason to suspect of deceiving him.

Ignorance of the meanings of words — a want of understanding — disposes men to take on trust not only the truths they do not know but the errors as well; and, what is worse, even the nonsense of those they trust. For neither error nor nonsense can, without a thorough understanding of words, be detected.

From the same source it comes that men give different names to one and the same thing according to the difference of their own passions. Those who approve of a private opinion call it 'opinion'; those who dislike it call it 'heresy.' Yet heresy means nothing more than private opinion — only with an extra dash of anger.

From the same source, too, it comes that men cannot tell apart, without study and great understanding, one action of many men from many actions of one multitude. For example, they cannot easily distinguish the one action of all the senators of Rome in killing Catiline from the many actions of a number of senators in killing Caesar. And so they are disposed to take for the action of the people what is in fact a multitude of actions done by a multitude of men, led perhaps by the persuasion of one.

Adherence to custom, from ignorance of the nature of right and wrong. Ignorance of the causes and the original constitution of right, equity, law, and justice disposes a man to make custom and example the rule of his actions, in such a way that he thinks unjust whatever it has been customary to punish, and just whatever the impunity and approval of which they can produce an example — or, as the lawyers (who alone use this false measure of justice) crudely call it, a precedent. They are like little children who have no other rule of good and bad behaviour than the correction they receive from their parents and teachers; except that children stick to their rule, whereas grown men do not. Having grown strong and stubborn, they appeal from custom to reason and from reason to custom as it suits them — backing away from custom when their interest demands, and setting themselves against reason whenever reason is against them. This is why the doctrine of right and wrong is endlessly disputed, by the pen and by the sword, while the doctrine of lines and figures is not. On that subject men do not care what is true, because it crosses no man's ambition, profit, or lust. For I do not doubt that, if it had been a thing contrary to anyone's right of dominion, or to the interest of those holding dominion, that the three angles of a triangle should be equal to two angles of a square, the doctrine would have been — if not disputed — at least suppressed, by the burning of all books of geometry, so far as the man whose interests it touched was able.

Adherence to private men, from ignorance of the causes of peace. Ignorance of remote causes disposes men to attribute every event to its immediate and instrumental causes, for those are the only causes they perceive. And so it happens that everywhere, men aggrieved by payments to the public discharge their anger on the publicans — the tax-farmers, collectors, and other officers of the public revenue — and side with those who find fault with the public government. By this they commit themselves beyond hope of justification, and so go on to turn also against the supreme authority, out of fear of punishment, or out of shame at having to accept pardon.

Ignorance of natural causes disposes a man to credulity, so that he often believes impossibilities: knowing nothing to the contrary, he cannot rule out that they might be true, since he is unable to detect the impossibility. And credulity, because men love being listened to in company, disposes them to lying. So ignorance, even without any malice, is able both to make a man believe lies and tell them — and sometimes also to make him invent them.
Anxiety about the future disposes men to inquire into the causes of things, because knowing those causes makes a man better able to order the present to his best advantage.

Curiosity — the love of knowing causes — draws a man from the consideration of an effect to the search for its cause, and then for the cause of that cause, until of necessity he must come at last to this thought: that there is some cause of which there is no prior cause, but which is eternal. This is what men call God. So it is impossible to make any deep inquiry into natural causes without being thereby inclined to believe that there is one God eternal — though men cannot have any idea of him in their mind that corresponds to his nature. For as a man born blind, hearing others speak of warming themselves at the fire, and being brought to warm himself at it, may easily conceive and become assured that there is something there which men call fire, and which is the cause of the heat he feels — but cannot imagine what it looks like, nor have an idea of it in his mind such as those who see it have — so also, by the visible things of this world and their admirable order, a man may conceive that there is a cause of them, which men call God, and yet still have no idea or image of him in his mind.

And those who make little or no inquiry into the natural causes of things — yet who, out of the fear that comes from this very ignorance of what it is that has the power to do them great good or harm, are inclined to suppose and feign for themselves various kinds of invisible powers, and to stand in awe of their own imaginings, and in time of distress to invoke them, and in time of expected good success to thank them — these men make gods out of the creatures of their own fancy. By this means it has come to pass that from the innumerable variety of fancy, men have brought into the world innumerable sorts of gods. And this fear of invisible things is the natural seed of what each man, in himself, calls religion — and, in those who worship or fear that power in some other way than he does, superstition.

And this seed of religion, having been noticed by many, has led some of those who noticed it to nourish, dress, and shape it into laws, adding to it, out of their own invention, whatever opinions about the causes of future events they thought would best enable them to govern others, and to derive the greatest use from their own powers.

title: Chapter 12. Of Religion
paragraphs: Since there are no signs or fruits of religion except in man, there is no reason to doubt that the seed of religion is also found only in man. It consists in some peculiar quality, or at least in some eminent degree of one, that is not to be found in other living creatures.

First, it is peculiar to human nature to be inquisitive into the causes of the events people see — some more, some less, but every person enough to be curious about the causes of their own good and bad fortune.
Second, when men see anything that has a beginning, they think it must also have had a cause that determined it to start exactly when it did, rather than sooner or later.

Third, whereas beasts have no other happiness than the enjoyment of their daily food, rest, and lusts — having little or no foresight of the time to come, for lack of observation and memory of the order, sequence, and dependence of the things they see — man observes how one event has been produced by another, and remembers in such things their antecedence and consequence. And when he cannot be sure of the true causes of things (for the causes of good and bad fortune are for the most part invisible), he supposes causes of them, either such as his own fancy suggests, or he trusts to the authority of other men whom he thinks to be his friends and wiser than himself.

[The Natural Cause Of Religion: The Anxiety Of The Time To Come.] The first two of these make for anxiety. For being assured that there are causes of all things that have happened up to now, or shall happen hereafter, it is impossible for a man who continually tries to secure himself against the evil he fears and to procure the good he desires not to be in perpetual concern about the time to come. So every man, especially those who are too provident, is in a state much like that of Prometheus. For as Prometheus (which, interpreted, means The Prudent Man) was bound to the hill Caucasus, a place of wide prospect, where an eagle feeding on his liver devoured by day as much as was repaired by night, so the man who looks too far ahead in care for the future has his heart gnawed all day long by fear of death, poverty, or other calamity; and he has no rest, no pause in his anxiety, except in sleep.

This perpetual fear, always accompanying mankind in the ignorance of causes — as though it walked in the dark — must have some object. And therefore when there is nothing to be seen, there is nothing to credit for one's good or bad fortune except some invisible power or agent. It was perhaps in this sense that some of the old poets said that the gods were first created by human fear; which, said of the gods (that is, of the many gods of the Gentiles), is quite true. But the acknowledgment of one God, eternal, infinite, and omnipotent, may more easily be derived from people's desire to know the causes of natural bodies and their several powers and operations, than from the fear of what might happen to them in time to come. For anyone who, from some effect he sees come to pass, reasons to its next and immediate cause, and from that to the cause of that cause, plunging himself deeply into the pursuit of causes, must at last arrive at this: there must be (as even the heathen philosophers confessed) one First Mover — that is, a first, eternal cause of all things — which is what men mean by the name of God. And all this without any thought of their fortune, the worry about which both inclines them to fear and hinders them from searching for the causes of other things, and thereby gives them occasion to invent as many gods as there are men who invent them.

As for the matter or substance of the invisible agents thus imagined, men could not, by natural reflection, hit upon any conception of them other than that they were the same as the soul of man; and that the soul of man was of the same substance as that which appears in a dream to one who is asleep, or in a looking-glass to one who is awake. Not knowing that such apparitions are nothing else but creatures of the imagination, men take them to be real and external substances, and therefore call them ghosts — as the Latins called them Imagines and Umbrae — and supposed them to be spirits, that is, thin airy bodies; and supposed those invisible agents which they feared to be like them, except that they appear and vanish as they please. But the opinion that such spirits were incorporeal or immaterial could never enter the mind of any man by nature. For although men may string together words of contradictory meaning — like Spirit and Incorporeal — they can never form any imagination corresponding to them. Therefore, men who through their own meditation arrive at the acknowledgment of one infinite, omnipotent, and eternal God prefer to confess that he is incomprehensible and above their understanding, rather than to define his nature by Spirit Incorporeal and then confess their definition unintelligible. Or if they do give him such a title, it is not dogmatically, with the intention of making the divine nature understood, but piously, to honor him with attributes whose meanings are as remote as possible from the grossness of visible bodies.

Then, as for the way they think these invisible agents brought about their effects — that is, what immediate causes they used to bring things to pass — men who do not know what we call causing (which is almost all men) have no other rule to guess by but observing and remembering what they have seen precede the like effect at some other time or times before, without seeing any dependence or connection at all between the antecedent and the subsequent event. And therefore from like things past they expect like things to come, and hope for good or bad luck, superstitiously, from things that have no part at all in causing it. So the Athenians, for their war at Lepanto, demanded another Phormio; the Pompeian faction, for their war in Africa, another Scipio; and others have done likewise on many other occasions since. In the same way they attribute their fortune to a bystander, to a lucky or unlucky place, to words spoken — especially if the name of God is among them — as in charming and conjuring (the liturgy of witches); to the point of believing that they have power to turn a stone into bread, bread into a man, or anything into anything.

Third, as for the worship which men naturally show toward invisible powers, it can be no other than such expressions of reverence as they would use toward men: gifts, petitions, thanks, bowing of the body, considered addresses, sober behavior, premeditated words, and swearing (that is, assuring one another of their promises) by invoking them. Beyond that reason suggests nothing, but leaves them either to rest there, or, for further ceremonies, to rely on those they believe to be wiser than themselves.

Lastly, as to how these invisible powers reveal to men things that will come to pass — especially concerning their good or bad fortune in general, or success or failure in any particular undertaking — men are naturally at a loss. Except that, being accustomed to guess at the time to come by the time past, they are very apt not only to take chance occurrences, after one or two encounters, as predictions of the like ever after, but also to accept like predictions from other men of whom they have once formed a good opinion.

And in these four things — belief in ghosts, ignorance of secondary causes, devotion toward what men fear, and taking chance events as omens — consists the natural seed of religion. Because of the different fancies, judgments, and passions of different people, it has grown up into ceremonies so different that those used by one man are for the most part ridiculous to another.

For these seeds have been cultivated by two sorts of men. One sort have nourished and ordered them according to their own invention. The other have done it by God's commandment and direction. But both sorts have done it with the same purpose: to make the men who relied on them more disposed to obedience, laws, peace, charity, and civil society. So the religion of the first sort is a part of human politics, and teaches part of the duty earthly kings require of their subjects. The religion of the second sort is divine politics, and contains precepts for those who have yielded themselves as subjects in the kingdom of God. Of the first sort were all the founders of commonwealths and the law-givers of the Gentiles. Of the second sort were Abraham, Moses, and our Blessed Saviour, by whom have been delivered to us the laws of the kingdom of God.

As for that part of religion which consists in opinions about the nature of invisible powers, there is almost nothing that has a name which has not, among the Gentiles, somewhere or other, been esteemed a god or a devil, or imagined by their poets to be animate, inhabited, or possessed by some spirit or other.
The unformed matter of the world was a god, under the name of Chaos.
The heaven, the ocean, the planets, the fire, the earth, the winds were so many gods.

Men, women, a bird, a crocodile, a calf, a dog, a snake, an onion, a leek were all deified. Besides, they filled almost every place with spirits called daemons: the plains with Pan and the Panises, or Satyrs; the woods with Fauns and Nymphs; the sea with Tritons and other nymphs; every river and fountain with a ghost of its own name, and with nymphs; every house with its Lares, or household spirits; every man with his Genius; hell with ghosts and spiritual officers such as Charon, Cerberus, and the Furies; and at night every place with Larvae, Lemures, ghosts of the dead, and a whole kingdom of fairies and bugbears. They also ascribed divinity, and built temples, to mere accidents and qualities — such as Time, Night, Day, Peace, Concord, Love, Strife, Virtue, Honor, Health, Rust, Fever, and the like — which, when they prayed for them or against them, they prayed to as if there were ghosts of those names hovering over their heads, letting fall or withholding the good or evil for or against which they prayed. They also invoked their own wit, by the name of the Muses; their own ignorance, by the name of Fortune; their own lust, by the name of Cupid; their own rage, by the name of the Furies; their own private parts, by the name of Priapus; and they attributed their pollutions to Incubi and Succubae — so that there was nothing a poet could introduce as a character in his poem that they did not make into either a god or a devil.

The same authors of the religion of the Gentiles, observing the second ground of religion — namely men's ignorance of causes, and their consequent readiness to attribute their fortune to causes on which there was no apparent dependence — took the opportunity to foist on this ignorance, in place of secondary causes, a kind of second-rank, ministering gods: ascribing fertility to Venus, the arts to Apollo, subtlety and craft to Mercury, tempests and storms to Aeolus, and other effects to other gods — so that among the heathen there was almost as great a variety of gods as of occupations.

And to the worship which men naturally thought fit to use toward their gods — namely oblations, prayers, thanks, and the rest already named — the same legislators of the Gentiles added images of them, both in painting and in sculpture, so that the more ignorant sort (that is, the greater part of the people), thinking that the gods the images represented were really included, as it were housed within them, might stand all the more in fear of them. They endowed them with lands, houses, officers, and revenues, set apart from all other human uses — that is, consecrated and made holy to these idols — such as caverns, groves, woods, mountains, and whole islands. And they attributed to them not only shapes (of men, of beasts, of monsters), but also the faculties and passions of men and beasts: sense, speech, sex, lust, generation (and this not only by mixing with one another to propagate the kind of gods, but also by mixing with men and women to beget mongrel gods, mere lodgers in heaven, such as Bacchus, Hercules, and others); besides anger, revenge, and other passions of living creatures, and the actions proceeding from them — fraud, theft, adultery, sodomy, and any vice that may be taken either as an effect of power or as a cause of pleasure; and all such vices as, among men, are considered to be against law rather than against honor.

Lastly, to the prognostics of the time to come (which are naturally only conjectures based on past experience, and supernaturally divine revelation), the same authors of the religion of the Gentiles added, partly on pretended experience and partly on pretended revelation, innumerable other superstitious forms of divination. They made men believe they might find their fortunes sometimes in the ambiguous or senseless answers of the priests at Delphi, Delos, Ammon, and other famous oracles — answers made ambiguous by design, so that the event could be claimed either way, or made absurd by the intoxicating vapor of the place, which is very common in sulphurous caverns. Sometimes in the leaves of the Sibyls (whose prophecies — like those perhaps of Nostradamus, for the surviving fragments seem to be of later invention — had some books of repute in the time of the Roman Republic). Sometimes in the meaningless speeches of madmen, supposed to be possessed by a divine spirit (which possession they called Enthusiasm); and these kinds of foretelling were called Theomancy, or prophecy. Sometimes in the aspect of the stars at one's birth, which was called Horoscopy and counted a branch of judicial astrology. Sometimes in their own hopes and fears, called Thumomancy, or presage. Sometimes in the predictions of witches, who claimed to confer with the dead — which is called Necromancy, Conjuring, and Witchcraft, and is nothing but trickery and collusive fraud. Sometimes in the chance flight or feeding of birds, called Augury. Sometimes in the entrails of a sacrificed beast, which was Aruspicina. Sometimes in dreams. Sometimes in the croaking of ravens, or the chattering of birds. Sometimes in the features of the face, which was called Metoposcopy; or by Palmistry, in the lines of the hand; in chance words, called Omina. Sometimes in monsters or unusual accidents — such as eclipses, comets, rare meteors, earthquakes, floods, strange births, and the like — which they called Portenta and Ostenta because they were thought to portend or foreshow some great calamity to come. Sometimes in mere lottery, like heads or tails (Cross and Pile), counting holes in a sieve, dipping into verses of Homer and Virgil, and innumerable other empty conceits. So easily are men drawn to believe anything from such men as have gained credit with them, and who can with gentleness and dexterity take hold of their fear and ignorance.

[The Designs Of The Authors Of The Religion Of The Heathen.] And therefore the first founders and legislators of commonwealths among the Gentiles, whose aims were only to keep the people in obedience and peace, have everywhere taken care: First, to imprint in their minds a belief that the precepts they gave concerning religion should not be thought to come from their own invention but from the dictates of some god or other spirit — or else that they themselves were of a higher nature than mere mortals — so that their laws might more easily be received. Thus Numa Pompilius pretended to receive the ceremonies he established among the Romans from the nymph Egeria; the first king and founder of the kingdom of Peru pretended that he and his wife were children of the Sun; and Mahomet, to set up his new religion, pretended to have conferences with the Holy Ghost, in the form of a dove. Second, they took care to have it believed that the same things were displeasing to the gods which were forbidden by the laws. Third, to prescribe ceremonies, supplications, sacrifices, and festivals, by which they were to believe the anger of the gods might be appeased; and that bad success in war, great epidemics, earthquakes, and every man's private misery came from the anger of the gods, and their anger from the neglect of their worship, or from forgetting or mistaking some point of the required ceremonies. And although among the ancient Romans men were not forbidden to deny what the poets wrote of the pains and pleasures after this life — which many of great authority and gravity in that state openly derided in their public speeches — yet that belief was always more cherished than its opposite.

And by these and other such institutions, they obtained, in service of their end (which was the peace of the commonwealth), this: that the common people in their misfortunes, blaming neglect or error in their ceremonies, or their own disobedience to the laws, were less apt to mutiny against their governors. And being entertained with the pomp and pastime of festivals and public games made in honor of the gods, they needed nothing else but bread to keep them from discontent, murmuring, and uprising against the state. And therefore the Romans, having conquered the greatest part of the then-known world, made no scruple of tolerating any religion whatsoever in the City of Rome itself, unless it had something in it inconsistent with their civil government. Nor do we read that any religion was forbidden there except that of the Jews, who (being the peculiar kingdom of God) thought it unlawful to acknowledge subjection to any mortal king or state whatsoever. And thus you see how the religion of the Gentiles was a part of their policy.

[The True Religion, And The Laws Of God's Kingdom The Same.] But where God himself, by supernatural revelation, planted religion, there he also made for himself a peculiar kingdom, and gave laws — not only of behavior toward himself but also toward one another. And thereby in the kingdom of God, policy and the civil laws are a part of religion, and so the distinction between temporal and spiritual dominion has no place there. It is true that God is king of all the earth; yet he may be king of a particular, chosen nation. For there is no more incongruity in this than that one who holds the general command of the whole army should also have his own particular regiment or company. God is king of all the earth by his power, but of his chosen people he is king by covenant. But I have assigned another place in the following discourse to speak more fully of the kingdom of God, both by nature and by covenant.

From the way religion is propagated, it is not hard to understand the causes by which it dissolves back into its first seeds or principles — which are only an opinion of a deity and of powers invisible and supernatural. These can never be so abolished out of human nature but that new religions may once again spring out of them, by the cultivation of such men as are held in repute for that purpose.

For since all formed religion is founded at first upon the faith that a multitude has in some one person, whom they believe not only to be a wise man, laboring to procure their happiness, but also a holy man, to whom God himself vouchsafes to declare his will supernaturally, it follows necessarily that when those who govern religion come to have their wisdom suspected, or their sincerity, or their love; or when they are unable to show any plausible token of divine revelation, the religion they would uphold must also be suspected, and (without the fear of the civil sword) contradicted and rejected.

What takes away the reputation of wisdom in someone who forms a religion, or adds to it once it has been formed, is the demand that men believe contradictions. For both sides of a contradiction cannot possibly be true; and so to enjoin belief in them is a sign of ignorance, which exposes the author in that, and discredits him in everything else he may propose as coming from supernatural revelation. A man may indeed have revelation of many things above natural reason, but of nothing against it.

What takes away the reputation of sincerity is the doing or saying of such things as appear to be signs that what they require other men to believe is not believed by themselves. All such doings or sayings are therefore called Scandalous, because they are stumbling-blocks that make men fall in the way of religion: injustice, cruelty, profaneness, avarice, and luxury. For who can believe that someone who ordinarily does the kinds of things that proceed from any of these roots really believes there is any such invisible power to be feared as he uses to frighten other men over lesser faults?

What takes away the reputation of love is the discovery of private ends — as when the belief they require of others tends, or seems to tend, to acquiring dominion, riches, dignity, or secure pleasure for themselves alone or especially. For what men gain advantage by for themselves, they are thought to do for their own sake, and not out of love for others.

Lastly, the testimony men can give of a divine calling can be nothing other than the working of miracles; or true prophecy (which is also a miracle); or extraordinary felicity. And therefore, in addition to those points of religion that have been received from people who did such miracles, the points added by those who do not approve their calling by any miracle gain no greater belief than what the custom and laws of the places where they were brought up have instilled in them. For as in natural things men of judgment require natural signs and arguments, so in supernatural things they require supernatural signs (which are miracles) before they assent inwardly and from their hearts.

All these causes of the weakening of men's faith are clearly apparent in the following examples. First, we have the example of the children of Israel, who, when Moses (who had proved his calling to them by miracles and by the happy leading of them out of Egypt) was absent only forty days, revolted from the worship of the true God that he had commended to them, and setting up (Exod. 32:1,2) a Golden Calf for their God, relapsed into the idolatry of the Egyptians, from whom they had been so recently delivered. And again, after Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the generation that had seen the great works of God in Israel were dead (Judges 2:11), another generation arose and served Baal. So that, miracles failing, faith also failed.

Again, when the sons of Samuel (1 Sam. 8:3), having been appointed by their father as judges in Beersheba, took bribes and judged unjustly, the people of Israel refused any longer to have God as their king in any way different from how he was king of other peoples, and therefore cried out to Samuel to choose them a king after the manner of the nations. So that, justice failing, faith also failed — to the point that they deposed their God from reigning over them.

And whereas in the planting of the Christian religion the oracles ceased in every part of the Roman Empire, and the number of Christians increased wonderfully every day and in every place by the preaching of the Apostles and Evangelists, a great part of that success may reasonably be attributed to the contempt into which the priests of the Gentiles of that time had brought themselves, by their uncleanness, avarice, and dealings between princes. Also the religion of the Church of Rome was, partly for the same reason, abolished in England and in many other parts of Christendom — so that the failing of virtue in the pastors makes faith fail in the people. And partly it was abolished because of the bringing of the philosophy and doctrine of Aristotle into religion by the schoolmen, from which there arose so many contradictions and absurdities that they brought the clergy into a reputation both of ignorance and of fraudulent intention, inclining people to revolt from them — either against the will of their own princes, as in France and Holland, or with their will, as in England.

Lastly, among the points the Church of Rome declares necessary for salvation, there are so many manifestly to the advantage of the Pope and of his spiritual subjects residing in the territories of other Christian princes, that were it not for the mutual rivalry of those princes, they might without war or trouble exclude all foreign authority as easily as it has been excluded in England. For who is there that does not see whose benefit it serves to have it believed: that a king has no authority from Christ unless a bishop crowns him? That a king, if he is a priest, cannot marry? That whether a prince is born in lawful marriage or not must be judged by authority from Rome? That subjects may be freed from their allegiance if, by the Court of Rome, the king is judged a heretic? That a king (like Chilperic of France) may be deposed by a pope (like Pope Zachary) for no cause, and his kingdom given to one of his subjects? That the clergy and the regulars, in whatever country, shall be exempt from the jurisdiction of their king in criminal cases? Or who does not see to whose profit accrue the fees of private masses, and the takings of purgatory, with other signs of private interest — enough to mortify the most lively faith, if (as I said) the civil magistrate and custom did not sustain it more than any opinion they have of the sanctity, wisdom, or probity of their teachers? So that I may attribute all the changes of religion in the world to one and the same cause: displeasing priests — and not only among Catholics, but even in that church which has presumed most of reformation.

title: Chapter 13. Of the Natural Condition of Mankind, as Concerning Their Felicity, and Misery
paragraphs: Nature has made men so equal in the faculties of body and mind that, although one man may sometimes be clearly stronger in body or quicker of mind than another, when everything is reckoned together the difference between one man and another is not so considerable that one man can claim for himself any benefit to which another may not equally lay claim. As for bodily strength, the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret scheming or by joining with others who are in the same danger as himself.

And as for the faculties of the mind (setting aside the arts grounded on words, and especially that skill of proceeding by general and infallible rules called Science — which very few men have, and they only in a few things, as it is not an inborn faculty nor acquired, like Prudence, while we are looking after something else) — I find a still greater equality among men than there is in strength. For Prudence is just Experience, which equal time bestows equally on all men in those things to which they apply themselves equally. What may perhaps make such equality seem incredible is only a vain conceit of one's own wisdom, which almost every man thinks he has in a greater degree than the common sort — that is, than everyone but himself and a few others whom he approves, either because of their fame or because their opinions agree with his own. For such is the nature of men that, although they may acknowledge many others to be more clever, more eloquent, or more learned, they will hardly believe there are many as wise as themselves. They see their own wit at hand, and other men's at a distance. But this proves rather that men are equal in this point than unequal. For there is ordinarily no greater sign of the equal distribution of anything than that every man is contented with his share.

From this equality of ability arises equality of hope in attaining our ends. And therefore if any two men desire the same thing, which nevertheless they cannot both enjoy, they become enemies. And in pursuit of their end (which is principally their own preservation, and sometimes only their pleasure), they endeavor to destroy or subdue one another. From this it comes about that, where an invader has nothing more to fear than the single power of one other man, if one person plants, sows, builds, or settles on a convenient spot, others may probably be expected to come with their forces combined to dispossess him and to deprive him not only of the fruit of his labor but also of his life or liberty. And the invader, in turn, is in the like danger from another.

And given this mutual distrust, there is no way for any man to secure himself that is as reasonable as Anticipation — that is, by force or cunning to master the persons of all the men he can, until he sees no other power great enough to endanger him. This is no more than his own preservation requires, and is generally allowed. Also, since there are some who take pleasure in contemplating their own power in acts of conquest — pursuing it further than their security requires — if others, who would otherwise be glad to be at ease within modest bounds, were not by invasion to increase their power, they would not be able for long to subsist by standing only on the defensive. Consequently, such enlargement of dominion over other men, being necessary for a man's preservation, must be allowed him.

Again, men take no pleasure (but on the contrary a great deal of grief) in keeping company where there is no power able to overawe them all. For every man expects his companion to value him at the same rate he sets upon himself, and at any sign of contempt or undervaluing he naturally endeavors, so far as he dares (which, among those who have no common power to keep them in quiet, is far enough to make them destroy each other), to extort a greater valuation from those who scorn him — by damaging them, and from others by his example.
So in the nature of man we find three principal causes of quarrel. First, Competition; second, Diffidence; third, Glory.

The first makes men invade for gain; the second, for safety; and the third, for reputation. The first use violence to make themselves masters of other men's persons, wives, children, and cattle; the second, to defend them; the third, for trifles — a word, a smile, a different opinion, and any other sign of low estimation, whether directly aimed at their own persons or by reflection at their kindred, their friends, their nation, their profession, or their name.

From this it is plain that during the time men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition called War, and such a war as is of every man against every man (a war of all against all). For WAR consists not in battle only, or the act of fighting, but in a stretch of time in which the will to contend by battle is sufficiently known. And therefore the notion of Time is to be considered in the nature of war, as it is in the nature of weather. For just as the nature of foul weather lies not in a shower or two of rain but in an inclination toward it over many days together, so the nature of war consists not in actual fighting but in the known disposition to fight, during all the time there is no assurance to the contrary. All other time is PEACE.

Whatever therefore follows from a time of war, where every man is enemy to every man, the same follows from any time in which men live without any other security than what their own strength and their own invention will furnish them with. In such a condition there is no place for industry, because the fruit of it is uncertain — and consequently no cultivation of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no convenient building; no instruments for moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and, which is worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death; and the life of man, “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.”

It may seem strange to someone who has not weighed these things carefully that nature should thus pull men apart and make them apt to invade and destroy one another. He may therefore, not trusting this inference drawn from the passions, desire perhaps to have it confirmed by experience. Let him then consider with himself: when he takes a journey, he arms himself and seeks to travel well accompanied; when he goes to sleep, he locks his doors; even in his own house he locks his chests; and this when he knows there are laws and public officers, armed, to avenge any injury done to him. What opinion does he have of his fellow subjects when he rides armed? Of his fellow citizens when he locks his doors? And of his children and servants when he locks his chests? Does he not accuse mankind as much by his actions as I do by my words? But neither of us accuses man's nature in it. The desires and other passions of man are in themselves no sin. Nor are the actions that proceed from those passions, until they know a law that forbids them — which, until laws are made, they cannot know. Nor can any law be made until they have agreed on the person who shall make it.

It may perhaps be thought that there never was such a time, nor such a condition of war as this; and I believe it was never generally so over all the world. But there are many places where men live so now. For the savage people in many parts of America, except for the government of small families (whose concord depends on natural lust), have no government at all, and live to this day in that brutish manner I described before. In any case, what kind of life there would be where there was no common power to fear may be seen from the kind of life men who have formerly lived under a peaceful government degenerate into during a civil war.

But even if there had never been any time when individual men were in a condition of war against one another, in all times kings and persons of sovereign authority, because of their independence, are in continual jealousies, and in the state and posture of gladiators — their weapons pointing and their eyes fixed on one another. That is, their forts, garrisons, and guns are on the frontiers of their kingdoms, and they keep continual spies upon their neighbors, which is a posture of war. But because by these means they uphold the industry of their subjects, the misery that accompanies the liberty of private men does not follow from it.

From this war of every man against every man, this also follows: that nothing can be unjust. The notions of right and wrong, of justice and injustice, have no place there. Where there is no common power, there is no law; where there is no law, there is no injustice. Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues. Justice and injustice are not faculties of either the body or the mind. If they were, they might be in a man who was alone in the world, just as his senses and passions are. They are qualities that relate to men in society, not in solitude. It also follows from the same condition that there is no property, no dominion, no Mine and Thine distinct — only what each man can get, and for as long as he can keep it. And so much for the bad condition that man is actually placed in by mere nature, though with a possibility of coming out of it, lying partly in the passions and partly in his reason.

The passions that incline men to peace are: fear of death; desire of such things as are necessary for a comfortable life; and a hope of obtaining them by their industry. And reason suggests convenient articles of peace, on which men may be brought to agreement. These articles are what are otherwise called the Laws of Nature, of which I shall speak more particularly in the two following chapters.

title: Chapter 14. Of the First and Second Natural Laws, and of Contracts
paragraphs: The RIGHT OF NATURE, which writers commonly call Jus Naturale, is the liberty each man has to use his own power as he himself wills, for the preservation of his own nature — that is, of his own life — and consequently of doing anything which, in his own judgment and reason, he conceives to be the aptest means to it.

By LIBERTY is understood, according to the proper meaning of the word, the absence of external impediments. These impediments may often take away part of a man's power to do what he would, but they cannot hinder him from using the power left to him according as his judgment and reason direct.

A LAW OF NATURE (Lex Naturalis) is a precept or general rule, found out by reason, by which a man is forbidden to do what is destructive of his life, or what takes away the means of preserving it, and to omit that by which he thinks it may be best preserved. Those who write on this subject usually confuse Jus and Lex — Right and Law — yet they ought to be distinguished. For RIGHT consists in the liberty to do or to forbear, whereas LAW determines and binds to one of these. So Law and Right differ as much as obligation and liberty, which in one and the same matter are inconsistent.

And because the condition of man (as has been declared in the previous chapter) is a condition of war of everyone against everyone — in which everyone is governed by his own reason, and there is nothing he can use that may not be a help in preserving his life against his enemies — it follows that in such a condition every man has a right to everything, even to one another's body. And therefore, as long as this natural right of every man to everything endures, there can be no security for any man (however strong or wise he may be) of living out the time which nature ordinarily allows men to live.

And consequently it is a precept, or general rule of reason, “That every man, ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre.” The first branch of this rule contains the first and fundamental law of nature, which is: “To seek Peace, and follow it.” The second contains the sum of the right of nature, which is: “By all means we can, to defend our selves.”

From this fundamental law of nature, by which men are commanded to endeavor peace, is derived this second law: “That a man be willing, when others are so too, as farre-forth, as for Peace, and defence of himselfe he shall think it necessary, to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men, as he would allow other men against himselfe.” For as long as every man holds this right — of doing anything he likes — so long are all men in the condition of war. But if other men will not lay down their right as well as he, then there is no reason for anyone to divest himself of his, for that would be exposing himself to prey (which no man is bound to do) rather than disposing himself toward peace. This is that law of the Gospel: “Whatsoever you require that others should do to you, that do ye to them.” And that law of all men: “Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris” (Do not do to another what you would not want done to you).

To LAY DOWN a man's right to anything is to divest himself of the liberty of hindering another from the benefit of his own right to the same. For he who renounces or passes away his right does not give to any other man a right which that other did not have before — because there is nothing to which every man did not have a right by nature — but only steps out of the other's way, so that the other may enjoy his own original right without hindrance from him (though not without hindrance from another). So the effect that accrues to one man from another's relinquishing his right is just so much diminution of impediments to the use of his own original right.

A right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it, or by transferring it to another. By simply RENOUNCING it, when a man does not care to whom the benefit of it accrues. By TRANSFERRING it, when he intends the benefit to some particular person or persons. And when a man has in either manner abandoned or granted away his right, he is then said to be OBLIGED, or BOUND, not to hinder those to whom such right is granted or abandoned from the benefit of it; and to do so is his DUTY, not to make void that voluntary act of his own. Any such hindrance is INJUSTICE, and INJURY, as being Sine Jure (without right) — the right having been previously renounced or transferred. So injury or injustice, in the controversies of the world, is somewhat like what in the disputations of scholars is called absurdity. For just as it is called an absurdity there to contradict what one maintained at the beginning, so in the world it is called injustice and injury voluntarily to undo what from the beginning one had voluntarily done. The way by which a man either simply renounces or transfers his right is a declaration, or signification, by some voluntary and sufficient sign or signs, that he does so renounce or transfer, or has so renounced or transferred it, to the person who accepts it. And these signs are either words only, or actions only, or (as most often happens) both words and actions. They are the BONDS by which men are bound and obliged: bonds that have their strength not from their own nature (for nothing is more easily broken than a man's word), but from fear of some evil consequence on the rupture.

Whenever a man transfers his right or renounces it, it is either in consideration of some right reciprocally transferred to him, or for some other good he hopes for by it. For it is a voluntary act, and the object of every voluntary act of a man is some good to himself. And therefore there are some rights which no man can be understood, by any words or other signs, to have abandoned or transferred. First, a man cannot lay down the right to resist those who assault him by force to take away his life, because he cannot be understood to aim by this at any good to himself. The same may be said of wounds, chains, and imprisonment — both because there is no benefit following from such patience (as there is from the patience of letting another be wounded or imprisoned), and because a man cannot tell, when he sees men proceed against him by violence, whether they intend his death or not. And lastly, the motive and end for which this renouncing and transferring of right is introduced is nothing else but the security of a man's person — in his life, and in the means of preserving life so as not to be weary of it. And therefore if a man by words or other signs seems to despoil himself of the end for which those signs were intended, he is not to be understood as if he meant it, or that it was his will, but that he was ignorant of how such words and actions were to be interpreted.
The mutual transferring of right is what men call CONTRACT.

There is a difference between transferring the right to the thing and transferring (or tradition, that is, delivery of) the thing itself. For the thing may be delivered together with the transfer of the right — as in buying and selling for ready money, or in the exchange of goods or lands — and it may be delivered some time afterward.

Again, one of the contractors may deliver the thing contracted for on his part, and leave the other to perform his part at some specified later time, being meanwhile trusted; and then the contract on his part is called PACT, or COVENANT. Or both parties may contract now, to perform hereafter; in which cases the one who is to perform in the time to come, being trusted, his performance is called keeping of promise, or faith; and the failure to perform (if it is voluntary) is called violation of faith.

When the transferring of right is not mutual, but one of the parties transfers in hope of gaining by it friendship or service from another (or from his friends), or in hope of gaining the reputation of charity or magnanimity, or to free his mind from the pain of compassion, or in hope of reward in heaven — this is not contract, but GIFT, FREE-GIFT, GRACE: words that signify one and the same thing.

Signs of contract are either express, or by inference. Express, when they are words spoken with understanding of what they mean. Such words are either of present or past time — as “I give, I grant, I have given, I have granted, I will that this be yours” — or of the future, as “I will give, I will grant.” Words of the future are called Promise.

Signs by inference are sometimes the consequence of words, sometimes of silence, sometimes of actions, sometimes of forbearing an action. Generally, a sign by inference of any contract is whatever sufficiently shows the will of the contractor.

Words alone, if they are of time to come and contain a bare promise, are an insufficient sign of a free gift, and therefore not binding. For if they are of the future, like “Tomorrow I will give,” they are a sign that I have not given yet — and consequently that my right is not transferred, but remains until I transfer it by some other act. But if the words are of present or past time, such as “I have given, or do give, to be delivered tomorrow,” then my tomorrow's right is given away today; and that by the force of the words, even if there were no other indication of my will. There is a great difference in the meaning of these words: Volo hoc tuum esse cras, and Cras dabo — that is, between “I will that this be thine tomorrow,” and “I will give it to thee tomorrow.” The phrase “I will,” in the former, signifies an act of the will present; in the latter, it signifies a promise of an act of the will to come. So the former words, being of the present, transfer a future right; the latter, being of the future, transfer nothing. But if there are other signs of the will to transfer a right besides words, then, even though the gift is free, the right may be understood to pass by words of the future. For example, if a man offers a prize to whoever comes first to the end of a race, the gift is free; and though the words are of the future, the right still passes — for if he had not wanted his words to be so understood, he should not have let the race run.

[Signs Of Contract Are Words Both Of The Past, Present, And Future.] In contracts, the right passes not only where the words are of present or past time, but also where they are of the future. For all contract is mutual transfer, or exchange, of right; and therefore one who promises only because he has already received the benefit for which he promises is to be understood as intending the right to pass. For unless he had been content to have his words so understood, the other party would not have performed his part first. For this reason, in buying and selling and in other contractual acts, a promise is equivalent to a covenant, and therefore binding.

He who performs first in a contract is said to MERIT what he is to receive by the performance of the other; and he has it as due. Likewise when a prize is offered to many, to be given only to the one who wins, or when money is thrown among many to be enjoyed by those who catch it, although this is a free gift, yet so to win or so to catch is to merit, and to have it as DUE. For the right is transferred in the offering of the prize and in the throwing of the money, though it is not determined to whom — that is decided only by the outcome of the contest. But between these two kinds of merit there is this difference: in contract, I merit by virtue of my own power and the contractor's need; in this case of free gift, I am enabled to merit only by the kindness of the giver. In contract, I merit at the contractor's hand that he should part with his right; in this case of gift, I do not merit that the giver should part with his right, but that, once he has parted with it, it should be mine rather than another's.
